title-group.article-title: Exposure-safety analyses of talazoparib in combination with enzalutamide in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) in the TALAPRO-2 trial

abstract.p: The TALAPRO-2 trial (NCT03395197) showed that the addition of talazoparib, a potent PARP inhibitor, to enzalutamide significantly improved radiographic progression-free survival in patients with mCRPC. Due to adverse events (AEs), approximately 62% of patients experienced dose interruption and 53% of patients experienced dose reduction of talazoparib in TALAPRO-2 trial. Hematologic AEs such as anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia were the most common AEs leading to dose interruptions or reductions. We investigated the relationship between talazoparib exposure as well as baseline patients/disease characteristics and Grade ≥ 3 anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia using graphical examination and Cox proportional hazard models. The results indicated that higher talazoparib exposure, Cavg, t, was associated with a higher risk of Grade ≥ 3 anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. Additionally, among the other baseline factors, we observed that higher risk of all tested safety endpoints was associated with lower baseline hemoglobin. In addition, higher risk of anemia was associated with lower baseline body weight and higher baseline lactate dehydrogenase. Higher risk of neutropenia was associated with lower baseline absolute neutrophil count and lower baseline body weight. These findings support the proposed dose modification algorithm as an effective approach for management of AEs.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Over the past decade, approvals of new treatments have improved outcomes for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) [1] but the disease remains aggressive and progression is inevitable highlighting the need for novel therapeutic options [2, 3].

Alterations in DNA damage response genes involved directly or indirectly in homologous recombination repair (HRR), including BRCA1 and BRCA2 [4, 5] can sensitize tumors to treatment with poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors [6, 7]. Preclinical data suggest an interplay between the androgen receptor (AR) and PARP, providing a rationale for their co-inhibition [8]. AR inhibition upregulates PARP activity and downregulates HRR gene expression [9], while PARP inhibition suppresses androgen receptor transcriptional activity and might help postponing progression [10, 11].

Talazoparib, a potent PARP inhibitor, was initially approved as a single agent at a dose of 1 mg once daily globally for the treatment of patients with deleterious or suspected deleterious germline BRCA-mutated human epidermal receptor 2 (HER2)-negative locally advanced/metastatic breast cancer and more recently was approved in combination with enzalutamide for the treatment of adult patients with HRR gene-mutated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC).

In the single arm phase 2 TALAPRO-1 study, talazoparib monotherapy administered at 1 mg/day had shown durable anti-tumor activity and a favorable benefit–risk profile in patients with heavily pretreated mCRPC with HRR deficiency [12]. The approval of talazoparib in combination with enzalutamide in first line mCRPC is based on the phase 3 TALAPRO-2 trial. TALAPRO-2 included two patient cohorts: an unselected all-comers cohort (Cohort 1) and a molecularly selected homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene deficient cohort (Cohort 2) with DNA damage response alterations in at least one out of a panel of 12 genes directly or indirectly involved in HRR [13, 14].

In vitro, talazoparib is a substrate of P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and breast cancer-resistant protein (BCRP) transporters and coadministration of P-gp inhibitors increased talazoparib exposures by 45% [15]. Prior initiation of TALAPRO-2 part 1, the in vivo effect of enzalutamide on talazoparib has not been evaluated. TALAPRO-2 part 1 was designed to determine the talazoparib starting dose based on safety and PK assessment of talazoparib + enzalutamide, including 13 patients dose with talazoparib 1 mg QD and 6 patients dosed with talazoparib 0.5 mg QD, in combination with enzalutamide 160 mg QD. The recommended dose of talazoparib in combination with enzalutamide is 0.5 mg once daily with further dose modifications allowed to manage AEs. This dose was selected with consideration for the impact of enzalutamide and the N-desmethyl metabolite of enzalutamide (both are P-gp inhibitors) on talazoparib pharmacokinetics (PK). Following oral administration of 1 mg once daily talazoparib in combination with enzalutamide 160 mg once daily, talazoparib exposures were higher (AUC0−24 h was 157% of the reported monotherapy) than previously reported at the same dose levels with talazoparib monotherapy, indicating that coadministration of enzalutamide increased talazoparib exposures [14]. The time to steady state of talazoparib was also prolonged from approximately 3 weeks to 9 weeks when administered in combination with enzalutamide compared to talazoparib monotherapy, reflective of the drug-drug interaction (DDI) effect of enzalutamide and N-desmethyl enzalutamide on talazoparib PK and consistent with the half-life of N-desmethyl enzalutamide (7.8 to 8.6 days). Enzalutamide and N-desmethyl enzalutamide exposures were generally consistent with previously reported values at the same dose level with enzalutamide monotherapy. A talazoparib start dose of 0.5 mg daily in combination with enzalutamide was selected for patients with normal or mild renal impairment as it generates similar talazoparib exposure levels to the recommended monotherapy dose of 1 mg daily. A talazoparib starting dose of 0.35 mg daily in combination with 160 mg daily dose of enzalutamide was selected for participants with moderate renal impairment. This reduced starting dose of talazoparib for moderate renal impairment participants was sufficient to approximately match talazoparib exposure achieved by the participants with normal renal function and mild renal impairment.

The efficacy and safety of 0.5 mg (normal or mild renal impairment) or 0.35 mg (moderate renal impairment) daily talazoparib doses in combination with enzalutamide 160 mg daily was established in patients with mCRPC in the phase 3 portion of TALAPRO-2 trial [14]. TALAPRO-2 showed that the combination of talazoparib with enzalutamide significantly improved radiographic progression-free survival by blinded independent central review compared with placebo plus enzalutamide among patients with mCRPC in both, an unselected all-comers cohort (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.63; 95% CI, 0.51–0.78; P < 0.0001), and a molecularly selected homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene deficient cohort (HR = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.33–0.61; P < 0.0001) [16].

The most common adverse events (AEs) in the talazoparib group (≥ 30% of patients) were anemia, neutropenia, and fatigue. The most common grade 3–4 adverse events (≥ 10% of patients) were anemia (185 [46%] of 398) and neutropenia (73 [18%] of 398) in the talazoparib group, with dose reduction and dose interruption allowed to manage toxicity. 62% of patients in the talazoparib plus enzalutamide arm of the all-comers cohort experienced dose interruption, and 53% of patients experienced dose reduction of talazoparib (58% dose interruption and 52% dose reduction in the HRR-deficient cohort), due to an adverse event (AE) [14].

Understanding the relationship between talazoparib exposure and response is critical to support the benefit-risk profile of talazoparib dosing recommendations and dose modification guidelines to manage AEs. The objectives of the analyses reported here were to characterize the relationship between talazoparib exposure and grade ≥ 3 anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia in patients with mCRPC regardless of HRR gene alteration status and to identify potential prognostic factors for the selected safety endpoints.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: TALAPRO-2 (NCT03395197) is a multinational, Phase 3, two-part study evaluating talazoparib in combination with the androgen receptor inhibitor enzalutamide as a first-line treatment in patients with mCRPC [13]. The protocol was approved by an independent ethics committee and all patients provided written informed consent. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, using Good Clinical Practice according to the International Council for Harmonisation Tripartite Guidelines. A schematic of the TALAPRO-2 trial is shown in Supplemental Figure S1.

An initial, non-randomized, open-label run-in period (Part 1, N = 19) was conducted to inform the selection of a talazoparib dose of 0.5 mg daily in combination with 160 mg daily enzalutamide (0.35 mg daily talazoparib for patients with moderate renal impairment). In Part 1, patients received either 1 mg or 0.5 mg talazoparib in combination with enzalutamide 160 mg daily. Part 2 was randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled, and evaluated the efficacy and safety of talazoparib in combination with enzalutamide compared with placebo in combination with enzalutamide. In Part 2, talazoparib was dosed at 0.5 mg orally once daily (or 0.35 mg daily for patients with moderate renal impairment) with or without food in combination with enzalutamide 160 mg once daily, and dose modifications were allowed to manage AEs. Thresholds for dose reductions were protocol defined, and reductions went from 0.5 mg to 0.35 mg to 0.25 mg to 0.1 mg once daily. Once the all-comers enrollment was complete, further enrolment was restricted to patients with HRR gene alterations (Cohort 2). Treatment continued until radiographic progression by blinded independent central review, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent.

sec.title: Study assessment
sec.p: In Part 1, PK samples were collected at pre-dose, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 24 h post-dose at Day 1 (Week 1) and Week 9. Additionally, PK samples were collected at pre-dose and 2 h post-dose at Week 5 and pre-dose at Weeks 13 and 17. In Part 2, PK samples were collected at pre-dose and 2 h post-dose at Weeks 3, 5, and 9, and pre-dose at Weeks 13 and 17. PK data were analyzed using a population PK approach [17].

Safety and tolerability were evaluated by assessment of AEs, physical examinations, vital signs, and laboratory evaluations. AE data were coded using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 20.0, and AEs and laboratory parameters were graded for severity using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 4.03. The period for treatment-emergent AEs was defined as the period from the first dose of study drug through 30 days after the date of the last dose of study drug or the day before initiation of a new antineoplastic treatment, whichever occurred first. Selected safety endpoints based on investigator reported TEAEs include the time of the 1st incidence of Grade 3 or higher anemia (hemoglobin < 8.0 g/dL), Grade 3 or higher thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 50000/mm3), and Grade 3 or higher neutropenia (neutrophil count < 1000/mm3).

sec.title: Talazoparib exposure metric
sec.p: With the exception of the patient whose safety event occurred first in the analysis population, all other patients had multiple Cavg, t values—each corresponding to a distinct safety event time observed across the population.

sec.title: Other prognostic covariates tested for association with the selected safety endpoints
sec.p: In addition to talazoparib exposure metrics, the tested potential covariates for safety endpoint analyses in the univariate analyses were preselected and included the following 4 categories:

list-item.p: Demographics: Age, baseline body weight (BWT), Race (Asian vs. Non-Asian).
Baseline performance status: Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG).

Baseline laboratory test values: baseline albumin (BALB), baseline alkaline phosphatase (BALK), baseline alanine aminotransferase (BALT), baseline aspartate aminotransferase (BAST), baseline bilirubin (BBIL), baseline lactate dehydrogenase (BLDH), baseline lymphocytes (BLYM), baseline hemoglobin (BHGB), baseline platelet count (BPLT), and baseline absolute neutrophil counts (BANC).
Prior therapy: prior radiotherapy (PR RADIO), Prior second-generation Androgen Receptor Pathway Inhibitor (ARPI).

sec.title: Visual examination
sec.p: An exploratory exposure-response (ER) evaluation was first conducted using a plot comparing Cavg, t values in patients with safety events to those without events at each time point when the events occurred. This is to examine whether there was a trend for patients with events to have a relatively lower or higher exposure compared with those without events.

sec.title: Cox proportional hazard model
sec.p: A univariate Cox regression analysis was conducted to screen for potential covariates and significant covariates were simultaneously included in a multivariate analysis. A visualized correlation plot was created to assess the correlation between covariates (continuous and categorical) before conducting a multivariate Cox PH analysis. Talazoparib exposure measure Cavg, t was retained in each step of multivariate analyses as exposure/response relationship is the main focus of the evaluation. In addition, Chinese vs non-Chinese patients (code as “CNPT) was added to the covariates in the multivariate analysis to assess the correlation between selected safety endpoints and Chinese vs non-Chinese patients to support the regulatory submission in China. The insignificant covariates (p-value > 0.05) were removed in each step while the exposure metrics were to be carried forward, until all the covariates included in the multivariate analysis other than the exposure metrics were all significant (p < 0.05). If the exposure metrics were significant, this model was considered as final model; otherwise, the exposure metrics should be removed to obtain the final model.

sec.title: Modeling software
sec.p: The exposure-response (E-R) analyses were performed using R software version 4.1.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). For model evaluation, the proportional hazard assumption was tested based on the scaled Schoenfeld residuals using the cox.zph function included in the survival package in R. Interaction terms may be evaluated to explore potential effect modification if deviations are observed for the scaled Schoenfeld residuals.

sec.title: Patient demographics and observed data
sec.p: Data for selected safety endpoints were available from a total of 417 patients in the talazoparib + enzalutamide arm from the TALAPRO-2 trial, including 19 patients from Part 1 (open-label) and 398 patients from Part 2 (randomized, double-blinded) Patients randomized to the placebo arm were not included in the exposure-safety analyses since they did not have talazoparib exposure. Among those 417 patients 2 patients received only enzalutamide and did not receive talazoparib. Three (3) patients had missing talazoparib exposure. The above mentioned 5 patients were not included in the ER safety analysis, leaving 412 patients [399 patients received 0.5 mg (normal/mild renal impairment) or 0.35 mg (moderate renal impairment) talazoparib; 13 received 1 mg talazoparib), who were included in the ER safety analysis. The baseline characteristics for all patients included in the ER analyses are summarized in Table 1. The number of patients who had treatment-emergent Grade⩾3 anemia, thrombocytopenia, or neutropenia is summarized in Table 2.

sec.title: Exposure-response analysis for anemia
sec.p: The potential ER relationship for Anemia was first examined by comparing Cavg, t between patients with and without Anemia events at each event day (Fig. 1). The grey boxplots represent the distribution of Cavg, t for patients without events at each event day, and the blue dots represent Cavg, t of patients with events. Patients with events (blue line) appeared to have higher exposure than patients without events (red line), suggesting that higher exposure may be associated with higher risk of Anemia. A Cox proportional hazard (PH) model was used to further evaluate the effects of talazoparib Cavg, t and other prognostic factors on anemia. In the univariate analysis, age, BWT, Asian vs. Non-Asian, BALT, BLDH, BLYM, and BHGB were significantly associated with occurrence of anemia (P ≤ 0.05). Both exposure variables Cavg, t and LogCavg, t were tested in univariate analysis and the results showed that higher talazoparib exposure (either Cavg, t or LogCavg, t as exposure metrics) was associated with higher risk of anemia. LogCavg, t had a lower p-value for significance than Cavg, t ;however, Cavg, t provided a more stable model with less deviation of hazard over time. The effect of talazoparib exposure on anemia, the main focus of the analysis, remained significant either using Cavg, t or LogCavg, t, indicating the robust assessment of the association between talazoparib exposure and anemia. Cavg, t was used in the subsequent analyses to improve model stability.

Prior to conducting the multivariate Cox PH analysis, we assessed the relationships among all candidate covariates. No significant correlations were identified, supporting the appropriateness of including these variables in the multivariate model (Supplemental Figure S2).

Significant covariates identified in the univariate analysis were included in the multivariate analysis. Here, age, Asian vs. Non-Asian, BLYM, and BALT were no longer significant. The final Cox proportional hazards model suggested that a higher risk for anemia was associated with higher Cavg, t, lower BWT, lower BHGB, and higher BLDH. (Table 3).

sec.p: To assess whether hazard ratio (HR) remains constant over time which is the assumption of Cox proportional hazard model for the final model, a diagnostic plot (Supplemental Figure S3) was constructed and showed no significant deviation from constant hazard over time for BLDH with p-value of 0.161. The hazards for Cavg, t (p = 0.01442) and BWT (p = 0.0037) appear to remain stable over time despite the small p values. However, a trend for higher hazard over time was observed for BHGB with a p value of 0.0050. Using logarithmic transformation of BHGB and including an interaction term between BHGB and time (or logarithmic transformation of time) did not correct for the non-proportional hazard over time for BHGB. The effect of Cavg, t on Anemia, the main focus of the analysis, remained significant with or without including interaction terms, indicating the robust assessment of the association between Cavg, t and Anemia. Therefore, the final model was considered adequate for describing the correlation between talazoparib exposure and Anemia.

sec.title: Exposure-Response for Thrombocytopenia
sec.p: The potential ER relationship for Thrombocytopenia was first examined by comparing Cavg, t between patients with and without Thrombocytopenia events at each event day (Fig. 2). Patients with events (blue line) appeared to have higher exposure than patients without events (red line), suggesting that higher exposure may be associated with higher risk of Thrombocytopenia. The relationship between Cavg, t and Thrombocytopenia was further evaluated using Cox proportional hazards model. In the univariate analysis, both Cavg, t and LogCavg, t were significantly associated with the occurrence of thrombocytopenia (p < 0.05). Age, BWT, BALT, and BHGB were also found to be significant. In addition, Cavg, t had a lower p-value for significance than LogCavg, t, thus Cavg, t was used in the subsequent analyses. Significant covariates identified in the univariate analysis including Cavg, t were included in the multivariate analysis. The variables age, BWT, and BALT were no longer significant in the multivariate analysis. The final Cox PH model suggested that higher talazoparib exposure and lower baseline hemoglobin was associated with higher risk for thrombocytopenia (Table 4). A diagnostic plot examining the assumption of a constant HR over time for the final model showed no significant deviation from constant HR over time Cavg, t and BHGB with p-values of 0.098 and 0.244, respectively (Supplemental Figure S4). Given the relatively low incidence of Grade ≥ 3 thrombocytopenia (7.8%) in the study population, the exposure–response analysis results for this endpoint should be interpreted with caution due to limited event data.

sec.title: Exposure-Response for Neutropenia
sec.p: The potential ER relationship for Neutropenia was first examined by comparing Cavg, t between patients with and without Neutropenia events at each event day (Fig. 3). Patients with events (blue line) appeared to have higher exposure than patients without events (red line), suggesting that higher exposure may be associated with higher risk of Neutropenia. The relationship between Cavg, t and Neutropenia was further evaluated using Cox PH model. In the univariate analysis, the results indicated that age, BWT, Asian vs. Non-Asian, BALT, BBIL, BPLT, BANC and BHGB were significantly associated with Neutropenia (p < 0.05). In addition, both Cavg, t and LogCavg, t were significant, and LogCavg, t had a lower p-value for significance than Cavg, t, thus LogCavg, t was used in the subsequent analyses. Significant covariates identified in the univariate analysis including LogCavg, t were included in the multivariate analysis. The variables including age, Asian vs. Non-Asian, BALT, BBIL, and BPLT were no longer significant in the multivariate analysis. The final Cox PH model suggested that higher talazoparib exposure, lower BWT, lower BANC, and lower BHGB were associated with higher risk for neutropenia (Table 5). A diagnostic plot examining the assumption of a constant HR over time for the final model showed no significant deviation from constant HR over time for LogCavg, t, BWT, BANC and BHGB with p values of 0.091, 0.104, 0.046 (borderline), and 0.079, respectively (Supplemental Figure S5).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Understanding the relationship between drug exposure and efficacy or safety endpoints is key to maximizing the therapeutic benefits of a drug while minimizing adverse events [18, 19]. The approved talazoparib monotherapy dose is 1 mg once daily, the MTD for talazoparib, for patients with advanced breast cancer and germline BRCA mutations. This was supported by the findings from ER analyses for efficacy and safety endpoints using data from EMBRACA and ABRAZO trials published by Yu et al.20 and Elmeliegy et al. [20], respectively. The results showed that higher talazoparib exposure was associated with both longer PFS and higher incidences of anemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, supporting the use of MTD to maximize the efficacy while utilizing dose modification (interruption and reduction) to effectively manage AEs. Talazoparib 0.5 mg once daily in combination with 160 mg enzalutamide once daily provided similar exposure as 1 mg talazoparib monotherapy, thus can be considered as the MTD for the combination. The ER analysis for efficacy using rPFS data from TALAPRO-2 showed that higher talazoparib exposure was associated with longer rPFS in patients with mCRPC when administered in combination with 160 mg enzalutamide, indicating that the talazoparib dose of 0.5 mg once daily (0.35 mg daily talazoparib for patients with moderate renal impairment) in combination with enzalutamide 160 mg once daily would provide the highest tolerable talazoparib exposure leading to optimal rPFS outcomes [21]. Anemia, one of the most common hematologic AEs for patients receiving talazoparib, is believed to be a mechanistic consequence of inhibiting PARP in eythrocyte precursors (e.g., Inactive PARP2 causes Tp53-dependent lethal anemia by blocking replication-associated nick ligation in erythroblasts) [22]. The current analysis explored the relationship between talazoparib exposure and Grade ≥ 3 anemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. The results of the analysis showed that higher exposure was associated with higher risks for Grade ≥ 3 anemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, indicating that lowering the exposure by dose interruption or reduction would lead to a lower probability of hematologic toxicities, and therefore dosing interruption or dose reduction is an effective way to manage these AEs. Overall, despite the high incidence of hematologic AEs, few patients in the TALAPRO-2 trial permanently discontinued talazoparib (10% with 4% due to anemia) because of those AEs, relative to 7% patients who permanently discontinued in the placebo + enzalutamide arm [16]. The low incidence of permanent drug discontinuation due to hematologic AEs suggests that these toxicities were effectively managed by dose interruptions and dose reductions. However, reduction to a lower dose should occur only if necessitated by AEs and according to the talazoparib dose modification guidelines since higher talazoparib exposure was also associated with longer rPFS.

The time-varying average concentration up to each selected AE event, Cavg, t, was used in the analysis to account for dose modifications over time due to reasons other than the safety event of interest and the impact of enzalutamide and its n-desmethyl metabolite on talazoparib exposure over time. Traditionally, the exposure metrics generally used in the E-R analysis is Cavg, which is the average exposure of the entire treatment duration. Hence, each patient will have a single Cavg value. For drugs with no or low frequency of dose modifications, Cavg will be the same or similar to Cavg, t after reaching steady state and suffices for the purpose of E-R analysis as either exposure metric adequately reflects the drug exposure over time. Alternatively, for drugs with a high frequency of dose modifications, Cavg, t at the time of each event could be considerably different than Cavg, with Cavg likely to be lower for patients with dose interruptions and/or reductions throughout the treatment duration, even before the event for patients occurs. Therefore, Cavg may not reflect the average drug exposure up to each event time. Dose reductions due to other AEs (e.g., diarrhea, fatigue) would lead to lower exposure and consequently a lower likelihood of experiencing the specific AEs (e.g., anemia, neutropenia). Moreover, the longer these patients receive a lower dose, the lower their Cavg will be, which results in even lower risk of developing the specific AEs. This trend (patients with lower exposure having lower risk of developing the specific AE, e.g., anemia or neutropenia) would result in exaggeration of the exposure-safety relationship [20].

In addition to the talazoparib exposure metrics, other covariates evaluated in the Cox proportional hazards models were identified for each safety endpoint. Lower baseline hemoglobin, lower baseline body weight and higher baseline lactate dehydrogenase were associated with higher risk of Grade ≥ 3 anemia. Lower baseline hemoglobin was also associated with higher risk of Grade ≥ 3 thrombocytopenia. Lower absolute neutrophil count, lower baseline body weight and lower baseline hemoglobin were associated with Grade ≥ 3 neutropenia.

In the TALAPRO-2 trial, higher incidence of Grade ≥ 3 anemia and neutropenia was observed for the Asian compared to the Non-Asian subgroup. Asian vs. Non-Asian was identified as a significant covariate in the univariate analysis for Anemia and Neutropenia. However, it was no longer significant when the significant covariates identified from the univariate analysis were simultaneously included in the multivariate analysis for Anemia and Neutropenia. Significant covariates (excluding Cavg, t) in the final models of Anemia and Neutropenia were compared between the Asian and Non-Asian populations, and showed that the Asian population had BWT skewed to the lower end of the BWT distribution of the overall population, potentially confounding the effect of BWT on Anemia and Neutropenia (Supplemental Figure S6). To tease out the potential confounding effect between Race (Asian vs. Non-Asian) and BWT, exposure-response analyses for Anemia and Neutropenia were conducted again after excluding Asian patients from the dataset. The result of the analyses showed that baseline body weight (BWT) is still a significant covariate impacting the risk of Grade ≥ 3 anemia and neutropenia. Lower BWT led to higher risk of Grade ≥ 3 anemia and neutropenia. The observed differences in the incidence of Grade ≥ 3 anemia and neutropenia between Asian and Non-Asian populations is likely due to the BWT differences between Asian and Non-Asian populations instead of a true effect of race.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The findings from these exposure-safety analyses support the proposed dose modifications from the recommended talazoparib dose of 0.5 mg once daily (0.35 mg daily for patients with moderate renal impairment) in combination with enzalutamide 160 mg once daily when required as an effective approach for the management of AEs.

notes.p: On request and subject to certain criteria, conditions, and exceptions (see [https://www.pfizer.com/science/clinical-trials/trial-data-and-results] for more information), Pfizer will provide access to individual deidentified participant data from Pfizer-sponsored global interventional clinical studies conducted for medicines, vaccines, and medical devices ( [1] (https:/accp1.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcph.1626) ) for indications that have been approved in the United States and/or European Union or ([2] (https:/accp1.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcph.1626) )\u0000in programs that have been terminated (i.e., development for all indications has been discontinued). Pfizer will also consider requests for the protocol, data dictionary, and statistical analysis plan. Data may be requested from Pfizer trials 24 months after study completion. The deidentified participant data will be made available to researchers whose proposals meet the research criteria and other conditions and for which an exception does not apply via a secure portal. To gain access, data requesters must enter into a data access agreement with Pfizer.
